title_candidates: AI tutors improve when you tell them not to over-help
summary: Ai2's TutorMoments study finds that AI tutors often do too much of a student's thinking, while a more explicit tutoring prompt improves their restraint.

primary_source.title: TutorMoments: Do AI tutors know when to help and when to hold back?
primary_source.author: Ai2
key_facts: The preview uses 462 de-identified tutoring transcripts and more than 1,500 teacher-annotated moments.
Seven models were evaluated with a vague tutoring prompt and a prompt that explicitly balanced support and rigor.
Every tested model improved with the more explicit prompt.
The evaluation measures simulated tutor behavior, not learning outcomes with real students.

supporting_sources.title: TutorMoments preview technical report
key_facts: The technical report describes the replay evaluation, annotation process, scoring limits, and preliminary findings.

supporting_sources.title: TutorMoments code
key_facts: Ai2 released the evaluation code and links to the preview dataset.

prerequisites: Access to any conversational AI assistant
One study question with a trustworthy answer source

steps.instruction: Give the assistant an explicit tutoring contract that requires one question or hint at a time and waits for the learner's attempt.
Solve one practice problem and verify the final reasoning against a trustworthy source.

references.title: TutorMoments: Do AI tutors know when to help and when to hold back?
references.author: Ai2

risk_flags: The preview measures model behavior with simulated students, not real learning outcomes.
The dataset focuses on U.S. elementary and middle-school math and should not be generalized to every learner or subject.
